problems.stem: A peer review of a classmate's storyboard reads, in full: 'This looks great, nice work!' Why is this not yet peer review?
options: It is too short to count as a sentence.
It offers no observation tied to a specific frame, principle, or learner outcome that the author could act on.
Praise is forbidden in graduate courses.
It does not mention the reviewer's name.
problems.explanation: Review is actionable feedback anchored to specifics. General praise gives the author nothing to revise.

problems.stem: A reviewer writes: 'I would have made the background blue and used a different font.' Why is this comment weak as design feedback?
options: Blue is a poor color choice.
It rests on personal taste rather than the shared criteria, such as Mayer principles or the stated learning objective.
Reviewers may not comment on color at all.
Fonts are never part of a storyboard.
problems.explanation: Useful feedback is anchored in the shared rubric and the objective. Preference comments do not tell the author whether a design standard was met or missed.

problems.stem: While reviewing a peer's storyboard, you notice Frame 4 is overloaded. You ask an AI tool to help. Which use respects the author's authorship?
options: Have the AI rewrite Frame 4 and paste its version into the peer's storyboard.
Use the AI to help you describe the overload precisely and name an option, then leave the revision choice to the author.
Ask the AI to grade the whole storyboard for the author.
Replace all of the peer's frames with AI-generated ones.
problems.explanation: Review surfaces issues and options; it does not take over authorship. The reviewer (and any tool the reviewer uses) describes the problem and lets the author decide.

problems.stem: As the author, you receive eight peer comments, two of which contradict each other. What is the most defensible way to handle them?
options: Apply all eight comments exactly as written.
Weigh each comment against the learning objective and constraints, then record which you accept, which you reject, and why.
Ignore all comments, since they conflict.
Apply only the comment from the highest-graded peer.
problems.explanation: Feedback is input, not instruction. The author judges each comment against the objective and documents the accept or reject decision, which is the design evidence.
